opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly one we're still thinking about. My best explanation is that these models aren't the blank-slate, learn-anything systems they're sometimes made out to be. They have inductive biases, and those biases seem to line up reasonably well with the kinds of structure human languages have.

Think about what our impossible languages actually did. In some, we shuffled the word order of each sentence, either completely at random or with a deterministic function. In others, we reversed the order of tokens, or introduced rules that depend on counting word positions instead of on linguistic structure. For example, a marker that has to appear exactly four tokens after the verb.

Natural languages don't work like that. Their dependencies tend to be fairly local: related words appear relatively close together, and the rules are defined over hierarchical structure, not linear counts. Many of our manipulations break that locality or make the patterns depend on arithmetic over positions. A transformer predicting the next token from left to right does seem to learn these less efficiently. You see it in the perplexity curves over training: the more natural-like languages get learned faster and end up at a better place.

There's also an information-theoretic angle. Random shuffles destroy a lot of predictable structure, so in a sense there's simply less learnable signal. But even when we control for that with deterministic, in-principle-learnable transformations, the model still struggles relative to the natural baseline. So it's not just entropy. Something about the structure matters.

We also did some interpretability work on the counting-based languages, using causal interventions. The model does eventually develop mechanisms to handle those rules, so it's not that they're unlearnable. They're just harder, and the solutions look different from what it develops for natural agreement patterns.

I'd be cautious, though. This doesn't mean GPT-2 has the same biases humans do, or that it's a perfect model of human language acquisition. What it does show is that the strong claim, that these models are equally happy to learn possible and impossible languages, doesn't really hold up empirically. Figuring out exactly which architectural properties drive these preferences is what I find most exciting going forward.

r002.rationale: It says related words in natural languages tend to appear close together and that manipulations breaking this locality make GPT-2 learn less efficiently.

r003.rationale: It links the difficulty with nonlocal patterns to a transformer’s left-to-right next-token prediction, communicating the hypothesis that the objective favors local structure.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. So the way I think about it is that the impossible languages we designed are all, in one way or another, violating things that are pretty fundamental to how natural language is structured. And GPT-2, even though it's a general-purpose sequence learner, has inductive biases that happen to line up with those natural structures, at least to some degree.

So take the shuffle languages, which are the most extreme ones. If you take English sentences and randomly shuffle the words, or even shuffle them within a fixed window, you're destroying the local dependencies that language models rely on really heavily. A lot of what a model like GPT-2 learns is this notion that nearby tokens are highly predictive of each other, and that the order of tokens carries meaning. When you break that, there's just less regularity for the model to latch onto, so perplexities go way up and learning is slower. And interestingly, the degree of difficulty scaled pretty nicely with how much we disrupted the order. Deterministic shuffles with small windows were easier than larger windows, and fully random shuffles were the hardest, which is exactly what you'd expect if the model is sensitive to locality.

Then the reversal languages are a bit more subtle. Fully reversing a sentence actually isn't that hard, because it's still a consistent, information-preserving transformation. But partial reversal, where we reverse after some marker token, was harder, because now the model has to track where that boundary is and essentially switch strategies mid-sentence.

And the hop languages, which were the ones I found most interesting, involve a verb-agreement marker being placed some fixed number of tokens after the verb. That's a counting-based rule, and natural languages basically never do counting like that. Agreement in real languages is defined in terms of hierarchical structure, not linear position. We did see GPT-2 struggle more with those relative to the natural control, and when we looked at the models with causal interventions, it seemed like the models were essentially developing workarounds, approximating the counting rule in a way that's less efficient than the structural rule it learns for the natural case.

So the short version is that GPT-2 isn't a blank slate that learns any pattern equally well. It has preferences, things like locality, a sensitivity to hierarchical structure that emerges from attention, and those preferences make natural-language-like patterns easier and the impossible ones harder. Which was really the point of the paper, to push back on the claim that these models can learn possible and impossible languages equally well.

r002.rationale: It explains that shuffling disrupts local dependencies between predictive tokens, reducing regularity and making learning slower.

r003.rationale: It describes GPT-2’s sensitivity to nearby-token predictiveness, but does not connect that preference to its autoregressive next-token prediction objective.

astra-6.text:
One possibility is that the model has inductive biases that favor the kinds of patterns we find in natural language. A transformer isn’t a completely neutral learner—its architecture and the way it’s trained make some patterns easier to learn than others. For example, predicting the next token can be easier when relevant information is nearby, and some of our manipulations disrupt those relationships.

But I’d distinguish the finding from the explanation. We found that GPT-2 had greater difficulty learning our impossible languages; that doesn’t establish that it has the same linguistic constraints humans do. The interesting result is that you can get a preference for natural-language-like patterns without explicitly building human grammatical rules into the model. Pinning down which architectural or learning biases produce that preference is a further question.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the important distinction is between a language being impossible for humans and being difficult for a particular model. GPT-2 doesn’t necessarily find those languages difficult for the same reasons a human would. It has its own inductive biases, coming from its architecture and the way it’s trained.

For example, if we transform a language in a way that disrupts local dependencies, we can make the prediction task harder. Information that would normally be nearby might now be much farther away, or the model might have to track positions to figure out which rule applies. So greater difficulty doesn’t, by itself, mean that GPT-2 has learned the same grammatical constraints that humans have. We need to understand which properties of those transformations are actually driving the difference.
